title: Neuron
summary: A neuron is a nerve cell built to send and receive electrical and chemical signals. Explore its branching dendrites, long axon, myelin insulation, and the synapse where it hands the signal off to the next cell — then see how that shape connects to everything from reflexes to memory.

compareCandidate.label: Neuron vs. a generic animal cell
compareCandidate.description: A generic animal cell (e.g., a skin or muscle cell) shares the same core organelles (nucleus, mitochondria) but has a compact, roughly round shape, unlike the neuron's long, branching, signal-carrying shape.

Signal transfer to the next neuron or muscle cell
plainLanguageExplanation: A neuron is a nerve cell — a tiny messenger that carries information through your body as fast electrical signals. Picture a tree lying on its side: the roots (dendrites) catch signals from other neurons, the trunk (axon) carries the signal down the line, and the branches at the far end (axon terminals) pass the message on to the next cell. Billions of these cells are wired together inside your brain, spinal cord, and nerves, and they're how you feel a pinprick, decide to move your hand, remember a birthday, or blink without even thinking about it.

whyItMatters: Every thought, feeling, movement, and memory you have exists because neurons are firing signals to each other right now. Understanding how a neuron works explains how reflexes protect you, why nerve damage or conditions like multiple sclerosis (which affects myelin) can slow reactions or cause numbness, and how medicines and even everyday things like caffeine change the way neurons communicate. It's also the starting point for understanding the whole nervous system, from touching a hot stove to learning to ride a bike.
